nodes.label: January SIBC missing Gold, Housing, NBFC, Tourism sub-classifications
nodes.description: January SIBC files structurally omit sub-classifications for Gold Loans, PSL Housing, NBFC credit, and Tourism. These series appear only in March files. January-to-January YoY comparisons for these categories are not computable, limiting the range of signals available in the majority of reporting periods.

nodes.label: PSL housing growth conflates reclassification with new lending
nodes.description: Following ceiling revisions, SIBC data cannot separate reclassified existing loans from genuinely new PSL-eligible origination. The reported growth number is analytically misleading — it includes a one-time stock reclassification that inflates the flow measure.
nodes.source: RBI PSL Amendment Oct 2024 + SIBC data step-up pattern
nodes.source_excerpt: Housing loan limits revised: metro ₹35L→₹45L, non-metro ₹25L→₹35L, effective Oct 2024
nodes.source_rationale: Single-period step-up magnitude with no new demand catalyst confirms reclassification as the primary driver

nodes.label: NBFC flows double-counted across services and end-use sectors
nodes.description: NBFC credit is reported as a services sub-category in SIBC, but NBFC on-lending reaches all sectors (retail, MSME, housing, vehicle). When NBFC credit accelerates, it inflates reported services growth while the actual economic activity is distributed elsewhere. Services credit is structurally overstated during NBFC expansion phases.

nodes.label: PSL sub-category totals are non-additive
nodes.description: PSL sub-categories (agriculture, MSME, housing, renewable, etc.) are not additive to a PSL total because individual loans can qualify under multiple categories and different targets apply to different bank types. A parent entity_psl aggregate node is intentionally absent from this model — adding it would imply an additive total exists, contradicting this gap.
nodes.source: RBI Master Direction — Priority Sector Lending
nodes.source_excerpt: PSL targets are bank-type specific; sub-category overlaps exist in classification
nodes.source_rationale: RBI Master Direction confirms different target structures per bank type; overlap creates non-additivity

nodes.label: MSME size definitions differ across SIBC sub-categories
nodes.description: SIBC applies the revised June 2020 MSME definition (turnover-based) for PSL but the earlier investment-based definition for industry credit sub-categories. Micro and Small under PSL and under Industry credit are not the same population. Cross-series comparison overstates apparent formalisation coverage.
nodes.source: MSME Ministry Notification June 1 2020 (Atmanirbhar revised definition)
nodes.source_excerpt: Revised MSME classification based on turnover and investment criteria effective June 2020
nodes.source_rationale: Different effective dates and criteria confirmed by regulatory text

nodes.label: Gold loan market entry / deepening for banks
nodes.description: Banks are taking share from NBFCs in gold loans, with banks growing faster. The product moat is operational (branch-level assay, safe custody, cash management), not regulatory — banks with branch networks can sustain competitive advantage. The growth trajectory is structural (collateral-driven), not speculative.
nodes.source: ICRA Research Report – Non-banking Financial Companies Gold Loans, September 2024
nodes.source_excerpt: Banks expanded at 26% CAGR vs NBFCs at 18% (FY2020-FY2024); PSBs share rose from 54% (Mar 2019) to 63% (Mar 2024)
nodes.source_rationale: ICRA data confirms bank share gain; operational moat inference supported by entry barrier structure

nodes.label: MSME origination infrastructure investment window
nodes.description: Banks that invested in MSME origination infrastructure (UDYAM-linked underwriting, GST-based cash flow analysis, co-lending rails) over 2022-24 are in a harvesting phase now. The competitive window for catch-up investment is approximately 2-3 years before the first-cycle cohort matures and saturation limits further marginal returns. Banks without this infrastructure will structurally underperform in MSME credit growth.
nodes.source: SIDBI MSME Pulse Special Edition Report, June 2025
nodes.source_excerpt: Formal credit penetration rising among UDYAM-registered MSMEs; GST-linked underwriting adopted by major private banks
nodes.source_rationale: SIDBI report confirms penetration trend; 2-3yr window is an inference from typical credit cycle maturation timing

nodes.label: PLI anchor-supplier chain finance
nodes.description: PLI scheme recipients have validated anchor relationships with tier-1 and tier-2 suppliers. Supply chain finance structures (invoice discounting, vendor finance, dealer finance) can be layered on these anchor-supplier relationships at lower credit risk than standalone unsecured MSME lending, because the cash flow is backed by a large anchor company.
nodes.source: PIB Press Release – PLI Scheme, PRID: 155082, August 2025
nodes.source_excerpt: By 2025 realized investments rose to ₹1.76 lakh crore as projects shifted to active implementation
nodes.source_rationale: PLI investment phase creates anchor-supplier relationships; SCF structuring is a standard inference from this supply chain visibility

nodes.label: EV-specific vehicle credit products
nodes.description: RETIRED at first FOUNDATION (2026-06-10). No external source verified for EV share of vehicle loans or EV-specific credit risk differentiation. No L1 signal separating EV from ICE vehicle loans. Returns only when EV share of vehicle loans is measurable in L1 (e.g., VAHAN registration data ingestion).
nodes.source_rationale: Zero sourcing, zero signal_ids, zero annotation_ids. Cannot persist across FOUNDATION cycles.

nodes.label: Renewable energy project finance — next capex wave
nodes.description: As the infrastructure supercycle completes, the next infrastructure credit wave is in solar, wind, and green hydrogen projects. Banks with project finance capability built on traditional infrastructure can redeploy that expertise. Government renewable energy targets create a regulatory pipeline that de-risks the opportunity.
nodes.source: PIB Press Release PRID 1888547 – Cabinet approves National Green Hydrogen Mission, January 4, 2023
nodes.source_excerpt: National Green Hydrogen Mission approved with target of 5 MMT annual production by 2030
nodes.source_rationale: Government renewable targets create a regulatory pipeline; bank redirection from traditional infra to renewables is an inference from capacity redeployment logic

nodes.label: PSLC market depth from PSL reclassification surplus
nodes.description: Banks that received a large reclassification-driven PSL surplus from the Oct 2024 ceiling revision can sell PSL Certificates to banks that are under-achieving on PSL targets. This deepens the PSLC secondary market and creates a one-time monetisation event for well-positioned banks.
nodes.source: RBI Master Direction – Priority Sector Lending; RBI PSLC guidelines (2016)
nodes.source_excerpt: Banks may sell PSL Certificates representing achievement of PSL targets to other scheduled commercial banks
nodes.source_rationale: PSLC mechanism confirmed; reclassification surplus creating a supply event is inferred from the Oct 2024 revision magnitude

nodes.label: CIC reporting compliance gaps creating off-balance-sheet credit risk
nodes.description: RBI Digital Lending Guidelines (2022/2025) require BNPL and digital credit to report to Credit Information Companies. However, compliance may be incomplete among newer digital lenders operating under first-loss guarantee structures or co-lending arrangements where the regulated entity's on-book exposure is partially shielded. If reporting gaps exist, the true unsecured credit stress is understated in bank balance sheets and in SIBC data.
nodes.source_rationale: Reformulated at first FOUNDATION. Original 'untracked channels' framing contradicted RBI DLG which mandates CIC reporting. Reformulated as CIC compliance gap in newer digital lenders — plausible but needs RBI Annual Report 2024-25 fintech compliance section as source. Cycle 1 of hypothesis clock.

nodes.label: Infrastructure repayment wave with insufficient new origination pipeline
nodes.description: Banks over-indexed to traditional infrastructure credit face a structural squeeze: the FY22-24 project book moves to repayment (compressing balances) while the next-cycle pipeline (renewables, data centres) is slower to ramp. Banks without next-cycle project finance capability face credit portfolio contraction.
nodes.source: RBI SIBC merged series — Infrastructure sub-sector YoY and FY acceleration signals
nodes.source_excerpt: Infrastructure credit FY growth sustained below system average across ≥3 consecutive periods
nodes.source_rationale: Multi-period deceleration pattern is consistent with operations-phase rotation

nodes.label: Services sector credit entry / scale-up
nodes.description: Services is the fastest-growing main sector, led by NBFC, trade and CRE credit. Lenders without a services origination capability are under-indexed to the highest-growth credit pool; the NBFC channel recovery is reopening intermediated flow.
nodes.source_rationale: Anchored to live SIBC sector trajectory.

nodes.label: Co-lending & warehouse-financing infrastructure
nodes.description: MSME formalisation makes small-borrower credit underwritable, but distribution is the bottleneck. Banks that build co-lending rails and warehouse-financing infrastructure with NBFC partners capture origination volume that pure balance-sheet lending cannot reach.
nodes.source_rationale: Anchored to live SIBC sector trajectory.

nodes.label: Infrastructure has no sub-classification despite being the largest industrial sub-sector
nodes.description: Infrastructure is the single largest industrial sub-sector by credit outstanding, yet SIBC provides no breakdown (roads, power, telecom, etc.). Sector-level signals cannot attribute infrastructure credit moves to a specific segment, limiting causal interpretation of the infrastructure cycle.

nodes.label: Industry sub-types do not sum to the Industry total
nodes.description: The by-type industry sub-categories in SIBC do not sum exactly to the reported Industry total (residual/unclassified credit). Sub-type shares and YoY computed against the total carry a small unattributed residual; partition-based decompositions are approximate.

force_instances.label: Gold price surge (2023–2026)
force_instances.description: Gold collateral is priced daily, so a rising gold price raises the loan value of an unchanged quantity of pledged jewellery. The book can therefore grow without a single additional borrower or gram — which is why gold loan growth cannot be read as demand. RBI's own Sovereign Gold Bond issue-price releases give the benchmark: the IBJA 999-purity average worked out to ₹5,611 per gram at the March 2023 issue and ₹6,263 per gram at the February 2024 issue, and gold has continued appreciating since. Loans against gold jewellery is the 'toward' entity in the personal-loans mix, so this force is load-bearing for that reading.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: An external commodity market price; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: RBI Press Release, 'Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme 2023-24 Series IV – Issue Price', 9 February 2024 (anchor); compared against 'Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme 2022-23 Series IV – Issue Price', 3 March 2023
force_instances.source_excerpt: works out to ₹6,263/- (Rupees Six thousand two hundred and sixty three only) per gram of gold
force_instances.source_rationale: Restructured 2026-09-10, not re-sourced — the figures were always real. The old excerpt asserted a PRICE SERIES across three dates, which single-page verbatim verification can never satisfy however true it is: an excerpt is checked against one page. The anchor is now one verbatim sentence from the February 2024 release, with the March 2023 release carried as a corroboration pair so the comparison stays auditable rather than asserted. NB the 2026-09-09 audit note claimed prid=55327 'returns no substantive content'; that was wrong — the page returns 7,413 characters including its own price sentence, and the note was a false negative of the audit's own region-finding. The third figure in the old excerpt (a ₹15,440 February 2026 redemption price) is NOT carried forward because it was not verified; add a current SGB release as a fresher anchor when one is to hand.
force_instances.source_corroboration_excerpt: works out to ₹5,611/- (Rupees Five thousand six hundred eleven only) per gram of gold

force_instances.label: RBI risk-weight hike on unsecured credit (Nov 2023)
force_instances.description: RBI raised risk weights on credit card receivables from 125% to 150% and on consumer credit from 100% to 125% in November 2023. Higher risk weights increase the regulatory capital cost for issuers, compressing origination economics for all unsecured retail products. A policy action with permanent structural effect until reversed.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: A discrete regulatory circular event; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: RBI/2023-24/85 DOR.STR.REC.57/21.06.001/2023-24 — 'Regulatory measures towards consumer credit and bank credit to NBFCs', 16 November 2023
force_instances.source_excerpt: it has been decided to increase the risk weights in respect of consumer credit exposure of commercial banks (outstanding as well as new), including personal loans, but excluding housing loans, education loans, vehicle loans and loans secured by gold and gold jewellery, by 25 percentage points to 125%
force_instances.source_rationale: Corrected 2026-09-09. The force previously cited NotificationUser Id=12569, which carries no risk-weight content at all; the circular is Id=12567. The claim was right and the citation was wrong, and nothing checked it because no gate verifies a force's excerpt against its page. Excerpt now verbatim and machine-verified.

force_instances.label: PSL housing loan ceilings raised (RBI PSL Directions 2025, eff. 1 Apr 2025)
force_instances.description: Raising a PSL ceiling reclassifies existing lending rather than creating new lending: a loan already on the book becomes priority-sector eligible the day the limit passes it. The 2025 Directions replaced the 2020 limits of ₹35 lakh (metropolitan) and ₹25 lakh (other centres) with a three-band table — ₹50 lakh for centres of 50 lakh population and above, ₹45 lakh for 10–50 lakh, ₹35 lakh below 10 lakh, against dwelling-cost caps of ₹63/₹57/₹44 lakh — effective 1 April 2025, inside the trailing-12-month window. Reported PSL housing growth therefore mixes reclassification with origination, which is what gap_psl_reclassification records.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: A discrete regulatory amendment to the PSL Master Direction; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: RBI Master Direction — Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Directions, 2025, 24 March 2025, effective 1 April 2025
force_instances.source_excerpt: Centres with population of 10 lakh and above but below 50 lakh 45 57
force_instances.source_rationale: Corrected and restored 2026-09-10. The force cited the SUPERSEDED 2020 Directions (id=11959) and dated the change October 2024; the operative instrument is the 2025 Directions (id=12799), effective 1 April 2025. NB the 2026-09-09 audit demoted this force on the reasoning that it had read dwelling-cost caps as loan limits — that reasoning was WRONG. Checked against the 2025 Directions, its ₹45L/₹35L figures are the new LOAN limits for the 10–50 lakh and sub-10-lakh bands. The claim was right and the citation was stale, so claim_type returns to inference.
force_instances.source_audit_note: 2026-09-09 audit: excerpt not on cited page. MORE THAN A CITATION PROBLEM: the excerpt claims PSL housing loan limits were revised to metro ₹45L / non-metro ₹35L, but the cited Master Direction states loans up to ₹35 lakh in metropolitan centres and ₹25 lakh in other centres, with ₹45 lakh and ₹30 lakh being the DWELLING-UNIT COST caps. The force appears to have read cost caps as loan limits. Needs re-sourcing against the current PSL Master Direction before the claim is relied on.

force_instances.label: PLI scheme capex drawdown phase (FY25–26)
force_instances.description: The Production-Linked Incentive scheme created a time-lagged capex investment cycle: approvals in FY22-23 led to active investment and credit drawdowns in FY25-26 due to the typical 2-3 year project implementation lag. Drives simultaneous growth in engineering, specialty chemicals, basic metals, and defence manufacturing credit — sectors that do not normally co-accelerate.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: Government scheme implementation phases and approval-to-drawdown lags; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: PIB Press Note – PLI Scheme: Powering India's Industrial Renaissance, NoteId 155082, March 2025
force_instances.source_excerpt: This momentum carried into 2025, with realized investments rising to about ₹1.76 lakh crore with 806 approved applications as more projects shifted from approval to active implementation
force_instances.source_rationale: Excerpt corrected 2026-09-10 to the page's own sentence. The 2026-09-09 audit first reported ₹1.76 lakh crore as absent from the page; that was a regex artefact of splitting on the decimal point — the figure is present and the force's claim was substantively right, only paraphrased. Machine-verified.

force_instances.label: MSME formalisation via UDYAM registration + GST data
force_instances.description: Formalisation makes small borrowers underwritable. The Udyam Registration Portal (from 1 July 2020) and the Udyam Assist Platform (from 11 January 2023) have brought 7.83 crore enterprises onto a government register as at 28 February 2026, giving lenders a verifiable identity and size classification where previously there was none. A registered enterprise can be underwritten, guaranteed and classified as priority sector; an unregistered one largely cannot. This is the mechanism behind Micro and Small credit growth that is not explained by demand alone. NOTE ON SCOPE: the register itself is the sourced part. The further claim that major private banks have adopted GST-linked underwriting is OUR inference about market practice, not something the cited release states, and it is deliberately not attributed to the source.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: Aggregate improvement in MSME underwritability via registry and tax data; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: PIB — Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, 'Formalisation of MSMEs' (Udyam Registration Portal / Udyam Assist Platform), 30 March 2026
force_instances.source_excerpt: over 7.83 crore enterprises have registered on URP and UAP as of 28.02.2026
force_instances.source_rationale: Re-sourced 2026-09-10. Previously cited sidbi.in/msme-pulse, a landing page with no quotable text, on a host that was not then allowlisted. SIDBI is now on the allowlist at T2 (statutory institution, but MSME Pulse is research, not a regulatory instrument); this force is nonetheless better served by the official register itself. Excerpt verbatim and machine-verified. The GST-underwriting half of the old excerpt was an authored generalisation and has been moved into the description as our own inference.

force_instances.label: Bank→NBFC risk weights restored to external-rating basis (RBI, eff. 1 Apr 2025)
force_instances.description: RBI raised risk weights on scheduled commercial banks' exposures to NBFCs by 25 percentage points in November 2023 (RBI/2023-24/85, Paragraph 2.B), raising the capital cost of the wholesale funding channel that NBFCs depend on. On 25 February 2025 RBI RESTORED those risk weights to the plain external-rating basis of the Basel III Master Circular, effective 1 April 2025 — reversing the constraint rather than easing it. Cheaper bank capital against NBFC exposure restores the wholesale funding channel, and bank credit to NBFCs is the SIBC line that records it. NBFC credit stood at 35.65% YoY (₹21.3 L Cr) at 2026-07-31, the fastest large block in the services cut, and the services mix is steered toward NBFCs (+15.9pp tilt). The restoration is in force across the whole of the July 2026 movement window.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: Aggregate NBFC channel capacity and credit availability; not measurable as a single isolated column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: RBI/2024-25/120 DOR.STR.REC.61/21.06.001/2024-25 — 'Exposures of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) to Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) – Review of Risk Weights', 25 February 2025
force_instances.source_excerpt: it has been decided to restore the risk weights applicable to such exposures and the same shall be as per the external rating
force_instances.source_rationale: Promoted hypothesis → inference 2026-09-09. The force was authored at FOUNDATION citing only the November 2023 circular that IMPOSED the constraint, with a rationale saying the recovery claim 'needs NBFC-specific data to promote to inference', and an excerpt that was a citation line rather than a quote (it does not appear on the page). The missing evidence was the reversal: RBI/2024-25/120 restores the risk weights effective 1 April 2025. Excerpt verbatim and machine-verified; the same page states 'The above instructions shall come into effect from April 01, 2025.', so the instrument is in force for the entire trailing-12-month window ending July 2026. Distinct from RBI/2024-25/119 of the same date, which covers microfinance only.

force_instances.label: MSP procurement volumes growing year-on-year
force_instances.description: Government MSP procurement agencies (FCI, state agencies) draw increasing bank credit each kharif season to finance grain purchases. As MSP prices and procurement quantities grow each year, the food credit cycle's peak and trough both rise — creating a secular upward trend on top of the mechanistic seasonal pattern. SOURCED 2026-09-09: the CCEA approved higher MSP for all 14 kharif crops for Marketing Season 2026-27 on 13 May 2026 (in force across the July 2026 data month), and the same release quantifies the procurement growth this force asserts — 8746 LMT of kharif crops procured over 2014-15 to 2025-26 against 4679 LMT over the preceding decade, with MSP paid to kharif growers rising from Rs 4.75 lakh crore to Rs 18.99 lakh crore across the same two periods. Both the price decision and the volume trend are external to the SIBC series.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: Government procurement volumes and MSP price decisions are external policy inputs; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: PIB — 'Cabinet approves Minimum Support Prices (MSP) for Kharif Crops for Marketing Season 2026-27', Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, 13 May 2026
force_instances.source_excerpt: During the period 2014-15 to 2025-26, procurement of 14 Kharif crops was 8746 LMT while during the period 2004-05 to 2013-14, procurement was 4679 LMT.
force_instances.source_rationale: SIBC data confirms the seasonal pattern and secular trend; FCI/CACP external source needed to promote to inference. Cycle 1 of hypothesis clock starts at this FOUNDATION.
force_instances.source_verification: excerpt verified verbatim against the live PIB page (re-verified through the unattended fetch path 2026-09-09)

force_instances.label: Infrastructure supercycle completing (FY22–24)
force_instances.description: Large infrastructure projects (highways, ports, power, urban) awarded in FY22-24 are transitioning from the construction/drawdown phase to the operations/repayment phase. This structural shift suppresses new credit origination even as existing project books remain large, creating a net drag on infrastructure credit growth. The next capex cycle (renewables, data centres) has not yet scaled to replace it.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: Infrastructure project lifecycle phases are not captured as a CSV column; the transition is visible only through aggregate credit deceleration
force_instances.source: RBI SIBC merged series (Jan 2024 – Apr 2026) — Infrastructure sub-sector YoY
force_instances.source_excerpt: Infrastructure credit FY growth sustained below system average across ≥3 consecutive periods

force_instances.label: ECLGS 5.0 guarantee window (May 2026 – Mar 2027)
force_instances.description: Union Cabinet approved Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme 5.0 on 5 May 2026 in response to West Asia crisis liquidity stress: 100% guarantee cover for MSMEs (90% non-MSMEs and airlines) on additional credit up to 20% of peak Q4 FY26 working-capital utilisation, capped at ₹100 crore, loans sanctionable until 31 March 2027 via NCGTC. Targets ~₹2.55 lakh crore of additional credit flow.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: A government guarantee scheme; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: Cabinet approves Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme 5.0 — Press Information Bureau
force_instances.source_excerpt: The scheme aims to provide credit guarantee coverage of 100% for MSMEs and 90% for non-MSMEs
force_instances.source_rationale: PIB release (cross-checked pmindia.gov.in) confirms the scheme window covers the current data period; guarantee-driven MSME lending is the documented ECLGS mechanism from the 2020-23 phases

force_instances.label: Collateral-free agri loan limit raised to ₹2 lakh (RBI, eff. Jan 2025)
force_instances.description: RBI raised the ceiling for collateral-free agricultural loans (including allied activities) from ₹1.6 lakh to ₹2 lakh per borrower, effective 1 January 2025 and in force through the June 2026 period. A higher collateral-free ceiling widens the eligible borrower pool and lifts per-borrower headroom under the Kisan Credit Card / PSL farm-credit route, expanding formal agriculture lending without new collateral. Policy activation of ch_kcc_psl_agri_limits.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: A regulatory ceiling change on collateral-free farm credit; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: PIB — 'Kisan Credit Card: Fueling Growth in Agriculture', 11 March 2026
force_instances.source_excerpt: increased from Rs 1.6 lakh to Rs 2 lakh per borrower
force_instances.source_rationale: PIB (official) confirms the collateral-free agri credit ceiling rose to ₹2 lakh/borrower effective 1 Jan 2025; the record PSL-agriculture (19.95% YoY) and agriculture (16.82% YoY) readings in June 2026 are the observable effect of the widened eligible pool.

force_instances.label: Vehicle Scrappage Policy incentives → replacement vehicle purchases (MoRTH, in force since Oct 2021)
force_instances.description: MoRTH's end-of-life vehicle regime pays owners to replace rather than retain. GSR 720(E) (5 Oct 2021) concedes up to 25% of motor vehicle tax on non-transport and 15% on transport vehicles bought against a Certificate of Deposit, and GSR 714(E) (4 Oct 2021) waives the registration fee on the same condition. The incentive is only claimable on a REPLACEMENT purchase, and replacement purchases are typically financed, so the regime lifts vehicle loan origination without any change in underlying demand for vehicles. It is modelled as a structural shift rather than a policy action because the instruments are standing rules whose bite grows with the scrapping network: 62 Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facilities established as at the source date, and MoEFCC's End-of-Life Vehicles (Management) Rules 2024 (S.O. 367(E), 30 Jan 2024) added Extended Producer Responsibility, putting scrapping obligations on vehicle producers. CAVEAT: the SIBC series reports vehicle loans as one line and cannot separate replacement demand from new demand, so this force is directional and cannot be sized from the data it explains.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: A statutory scrapping-incentive regime and the build-out of scrapping facilities; neither is a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: PIB — 'Vehicle Scrappage Policy, 2021', Ministry of Road Transport & Highways, 8 August 2024 (Lok Sabha written reply)
force_instances.source_excerpt: MoRTH has issued GSR 720 (E) dated 5th October 2021 to provide concession in the Motor Vehicle Tax of up to 25% in case of non-transport vehicles
force_instances.source_rationale: PIB (official) records the standing scrapping incentives and confirms they remain in force, with the 2024 EPR rules extending the regime rather than withdrawing it. Vehicle loans grew 18.78% YoY to ₹7.65L Cr at 2026-07-31. Excerpt re-verified verbatim on the live page 2026-09-09, both in the browser and through the unattended fetch path.

force_instances.label: PSL education loan ceiling raised ₹20L → ₹25L (RBI PSL Directions 2025, eff. 1 Apr 2025)
force_instances.description: A higher PSL ceiling brings larger education loans inside priority-sector classification, so reported PSL education credit rises partly by reclassification rather than by new lending. The 2025 Directions raise the per-individual limit from ₹20 lakh under the 2020 Directions to ₹25 lakh, effective 1 April 2025 — inside the trailing-12-month window. PSL educational loans grew 16.70% YoY at 2026-07-31 against 13.71% for the personal-loans education line, and the gap between the two is where the reclassification sits.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: A regulatory classification threshold; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: RBI Master Direction — Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Directions, 2025, 24 March 2025, effective 1 April 2025
force_instances.source_excerpt: not exceeding ₹25 lakh will be considered as eligible for priority sector classification
force_instances.source_rationale: Authored 2026-09-10 from S4 proposal [4] (2026-08-31), which sought an education interest-subvention instrument. The subvention was not the change in this window; the PSL ceiling was. Baseline ₹20 lakh verified on the superseded 2020 Directions (id=11959); excerpt machine-verified.

force_instances.label: PSL renewable-energy loan ceiling raised ₹30cr → ₹35cr (RBI PSL Directions 2025, eff. 1 Apr 2025)
force_instances.description: A higher PSL ceiling admits larger renewable-energy projects to priority-sector classification, lifting reported PSL renewable credit through eligibility as well as origination. The 2025 Directions raise the per-borrower limit for renewable-energy power generators and public utilities from ₹30 crore under the 2020 Directions to ₹35 crore, effective 1 April 2025 — inside the trailing-12-month window; the individual-household limit stays ₹10 lakh. PSL renewable energy grew 31.70% YoY at 2026-07-31, the fastest PSL sub-category, though on a small ₹16,014 crore book — the speed should never be published without that size.
force_instances.non_observable_reason: A regulatory classification threshold; not a time-series column in the SIBC CSV
force_instances.source: RBI Master Direction — Reserve Bank of India (Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) Directions, 2025, 24 March 2025, effective 1 April 2025
force_instances.source_excerpt: Bank loans up to a limit of ₹35 crore to borrowers for renewable energy-based power generators
force_instances.source_rationale: Authored 2026-09-10 from S4 proposal [7] (2026-08-31), which sought a rooftop-solar subsidy instrument (MNRE, not allowlisted). The PSL ceiling is the better-evidenced driver and is on an official host. Baseline ₹30 crore verified on the superseded 2020 Directions (id=11959).

loops.label: PLI Supply Chain Reinforcing Loop
loops.closure_note: Closes externally as production volume growth leads to approval of subsequent PLI cohorts, sustaining the investment cycle
loops.description: PLI capex investment drives metals and chemicals credit, which feed engineering manufacturing credit growth, which drives overall industry credit. As production capacity grows and PLI targets are achieved, subsequent policy cohorts sustain and extend the cycle.

loops.label: MSME Formalisation Reinforcing Loop
loops.closure_note: Closes externally as successful MSME credit access enables business expansion and upstream supplier formalisation, compounding the registry effect
loops.description: MSME formalisation via UDYAM + GST data makes MSMEs underwritable, driving credit growth. Successful credit access enables MSME business expansion and formalization of additional supply chain participants. The growing pool of UDYAM-registered MSMEs reinforces the origination opportunity.

loops.label: Unsecured Credit Rerouting Balancing Loop
loops.closure_note: Closes externally when regulatory pressure eases (risk weights reversed) or when secured credit capacity saturates, allowing unsecured credit to recover
loops.description: Risk-weight pressure suppresses unsecured credit (credit cards, consumer durables). Displaced household demand reroutes to secured gold loans. As secured credit absorbs the displaced demand, the overall retail credit mix rebalances. The pressure creates its own relief valve — a balancing loop that dampens the impact on total retail credit.

loops.label: Infrastructure Cycle Transition Balancing Loop
loops.closure_note: Closes as renewable energy and next-generation infrastructure investment creates a new capex cycle that absorbs the capacity displaced by traditional infra repayment
loops.description: Infrastructure supercycle completion suppresses traditional infra credit, creating repayment pressure for banks. This same capital redeployment creates a renewable energy project finance opportunity — the next infrastructure wave. The balancing character: as traditional infra contracts, the conditions for the next capex cycle strengthen.
